meta.title: The gas wholesale market
meta.subtitle: How the GB gas price forms, driver by driver -- and why a GB gas price is usually a continental and global LNG price.
meta.one_line: GB gas trades at the National Balancing Point, a virtual point where all gas in the network is deemed to be. Its price is set by the last molecule GB needs -- usually a flexible LNG cargo or a flow through the pipes from the continent -- so it tracks the Dutch TTF hub and the Asian LNG price, not any GB cost of production. Gas matters twice to a supplier: it sells it, and it is the fuel of the plant that usually sets the electricity price.
meta.wall_placement: Public-reality commons only. Everything on this page is a published feature of the GB energy market, readable by anyone — so it is readable by the simulated company too, the same way a real supplier reads the codes and the market reports. Nothing here is an internal of the simulation.

headline.heading: The claim, in one sentence
headline.body: The GB gas price is set at the margin by imports -- LNG cargoes competing with Asia and flows through the pipes to Belgium and the Netherlands -- so NBP moves with the continental TTF price and the global LNG price, except when the interconnectors fill and GB decouples, as it did in 2022.

plain.heading: In plain terms
plain.body:
Britain produces under half the gas it burns. In 2019 the North Sea supplied about 46%, Norway's pipelines 32% and LNG ships 20%; in 2024 it was 43%, 43% and 14% (DESNZ, DUKES 2026, chapter 4).

North Sea and Norwegian gas flows at a fairly steady rate whatever the price. The gas that changes from day to day and season to season is LNG, and gas moving through two pipes to the continent: the Interconnector to Zeebrugge (IUK) and BBL to the Netherlands. Those are the molecules that set the price. An LNG cargo goes wherever it is paid most, so GB's price has to compete with Asia's. Gas moves through the pipes until the GB and continental prices are within the cost of moving it, so most of the time NBP is a continental price.

Britain stores very little gas. After Centrica stopped refilling Rough in 2017, GB storage was about 1.3 bcm in 2019, about 5% of a year's demand against an EU average of 29%. It has risen to about 3.2 bcm since Rough was partly reopened. So GB meets winter by importing more at the continent's winter price, and a cold week reaches the price quickly.

Demand swings with the weather: households are about a third of GB gas use, almost all of it heating, and power stations about a quarter to a third, burning more when the wind drops.

theory.heading: How it works
theory.body:
**The price and the market.** NBP is a virtual point: gas anywhere on the National Transmission System is deemed to be there, and it trades from within-day out to seasons. The System Average Price (SAP) is the volume-weighted average of the day's on-the-day market trades, published by National Gas. Shippers balance over the gas day, and a shipper out of balance is cashed out at the system marginal buy or sell price, which sit outside SAP.

**1. North Sea (UKCS) production** -- 344 TWh in 2024, about 27% of its 2000 peak. It flows to its own plans and barely responds to price, so it sets how much GB must import, not the price. Its decline means more of each winter day is met by the price-setting imports.

**2. Norwegian pipelines** -- the largest import: 76% of imports in 2024. Langeled, Vesterled, Tampen and others run near capacity, so Norway moves the price through maintenance (mainly late summer) and outages. Because Norway also supplies the continent, its outages move NBP and TTF together.

**3. LNG and the global market** -- the swing supply. GB has about 156 mcm/day of import terminal capacity (Grain, South Hook, Dragon), large against its needs. A flexible cargo goes where it earns most after shipping. When Asia's price (JKM) is high, NBP must rise to attract cargoes; when LNG is plentiful, GB is where surplus lands. US cargoes were half of GB's LNG in 2022 and 68% in 2024.

**4. Storage, and the loss of Rough** -- continental Europe stores a quarter or more of its annual demand and runs a large summer-to-winter arbitrage. GB lost its only large seasonal store in 2017 and kept fast-cycle salt caverns that smooth days, not seasons. So the GB winter premium is largely the continent's, plus a cold-day premium when its own pipes are full.

**5. Interconnection to the continent** -- IUK (58 mcm/d in, 55 out) and BBL (22 in, 15 out, reversible only since July 2019) arbitrage NBP against Zeebrugge and TTF to within a few pence a therm. When they fill, the coupling breaks. In summer 2022 GB landed more LNG than it could burn or export: exports reached a record 260 TWh, a quarter of supply, and NBP traded tens of euros per MWh below TTF.

**6. Weather-driven demand** -- 687 TWh in 2024, down from 854 TWh in 2019. National Gas forecasts household demand from a composite weather variable (temperature, wind chill), and gas-for-power follows the electricity residual, so a cold, still day raises both. A forecast cold spell moves forward and day-ahead prices; an unforecast one lands in the within-day price and SAP.

**7. 2021-23: every driver at once** -- low EU storage after 2021, Asian LNG demand, Russian flows to Europe down about 25% in late 2021, then about 50% in 2022 with Nord Stream stopped. Europe outbid Asia for LNG, and TTF went from a 12% discount to Asian LNG to a 19% premium (IEA). GB imported that price in winter, and in summer it decoupled below it.

**The link to power.** A gas plant at about 50% efficiency turns £1/MWh on gas into about £2/MWh on power in the hours gas is marginal, before carbon. That is the electricity page's subject.

expected_shape.heading: What the data should look like
expected_shape.body:
**Level follows TTF, except when the pipes are full.** Outside 2021-22 the GB and TTF monthly levels should agree to within a few per cent. In 2022 GB should sit well below TTF in summer.

**Persistent daily movement.** Within a month GB SAP moved about 7% a day before the crisis, 17% in it and 4% after (SD of daily log returns), and a day's price is mostly yesterday's: lag-1 autocorrelation 0.91-0.98. That is the shape of persistent supply and weather shocks absorbed by thin storage, not independent noise.

**A modest winter premium.** GB monthly means ran about 16-20% higher in winter than summer in each regime: 1.16 before the crisis, 1.19 in it, 1.20 after.

**Cold-snap spikes in the within-day price.** 1 Mar 2018 (the Beast from the East) is the archetype: storage at its lowest since 2010 and a SAP of £127/MWh.

live_evidence.heading: What this simulation actually does
live_evidence.body:
Graded 24 Nov 2026 against GB SAP, by regime, with the predictions filed first (pre-registration and result in docs/staging/records/).

**The world's gas record** -- what every run reads -- is a monthly European (TTF) price, spread flat over each month's days. Its level is right outside the crisis: monthly error £0.58/MWh in 2018-mid 2021 and £1.27/MWh from mid 2023. In the crisis it is £16.40, almost all of it 2022: from June to September 2022 the world priced gas at £139.79/MWh against GB's £87.02. That is the interconnector decoupling in driver 5, which a TTF price cannot show. Within a month the world's price does not move at all, against GB's 4-17% a day, so nothing the world's weather does reaches its gas price.

A daily GB series (SAP from 2018) has been spliced in and is ready. Switching the world to it is held until a comparison already under way has read, so both arms of that comparison see the same world.

**The forward-year gas draw** draws each day independently: daily movement 13.5 times GB's, no persistence (lag-1 0.005 against 0.984), and no seasonal or weather term. It is filed as a defect to fix with the electricity rebuild. Its level is the director's curriculum and is not graded here.

residuals.heading: What this page does not settle
residuals.body:
What is not yet established (each is a named GAP on the source page): the normal NBP-TTF basis as a daily series, and daily flows through IUK and BBL; Ofgem's published NBP summer-winter spread; an Asian LNG (JKM) series; any published price response of GB gas to temperature or demand; daily Norwegian flows and outages; and a daily GB price before 2018.

Nor does any source read settle how much of the 2021-22 level was fundamentals and how much was risk being repriced. The world replays the record and takes no view. Forward years will have to take one, and none yet does.

SAP is a within-day price. A supplier buys forward and day-ahead, and on a stress day the two can be far apart. No free daily day-ahead NBP series has been read.

scope_delta.heading: Where the simulation stops
scope_delta.body: No shipper-level daily balancing: gas is settled, but the company does not nominate and is not cashed out at the system marginal prices. No storage, LNG, Norwegian-flow or interconnector state in the world. The world's historical gas price carries the global level and nothing below a month, and its forward draw carries none of the drivers above. The electricity page (merit order, interconnectors, CfD and RO, nuclear, carbon) is the next piece of work, and the rebuild of both price draws comes after it.
